extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph (means-or-step-plus-function) including identification, claim construction, prior art search, making a prima facie case of equivalence, and related 112 first/second paragraph issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation limited to corresponding structure/material/acts and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. §112, 6th paragraph "means or step plus function" limitation in a claim must be interpreted as limited to the corresponding structure, materials or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective immediately (per In re Donaldson), examiners shall not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification corresponding to means-plus-function language when rendering a patentability determination. This changes prior practice of reading such limitations to cover any prior art means that performs the function without regard to equivalence to disclosed structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify means/step-plus-function by functionally-defined claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation falls under §112, 6th paragraph if the element in the claim is set forth, at least in part, by the function it performs as opposed to the specific structure, material, or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no magic phrase required; examples include: 'jet driving device so constructed and located on the rotor as to drive the rotor' (means unnecessary), 'printing means'/'means for printing', 'force generating means adapted to provide...', 'call cost register means, including a digital display for providing a substantially instantaneous display for...', reducing the coefficient of friction of the resulting film (step-plus-function), and 'raising the pH of the resultant pulp to about 5.0 to precipitate...' (step-plus-function). If unclear whether a limitation falls within §112, 6th paragraph, a rejection under §112, second paragraph may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If specification defines limitation, give that meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification defines what is meant by the limitation for the purposes of the claimed invention, the examiner should interpret the limitation as having that meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no definition is provided, examiners must exercise judgment in determining scope of the limitation; interpretation should be consistent with specification disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prior art search unchanged: prior art must perform identical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of a prior art reference to a means- or step-plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donaldson does not substantially change the scope of the search; however, once identity of function is found, examiner carries initial burden to show that the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the structure, material, or acts described in the specification corresponding to the claimed limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a prima facie case of equivalence when prior art performs claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art element performs the function specified in the claim, and is not excluded by any explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, the examiner should infer that the prior art element is an equivalent and conclude that the claimed limitation is anticipated by the prior art element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the examiner makes this inference, the burden shifts to the applicant to show that the prior art element is not an equivalent of the structure, material or acts disclosed in the application (citing In re Mulder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bears burden to prove non-equivalence once examiner makes prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: After examiner infers equivalence, applicant may provide reasons or evidence why the prior art element should not be considered an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible applicant reasons include: teachings in the specification that particular prior art is not equivalent, teachings in the prior art reference indicating non-equivalence, or Rule 132 affidavit evidence of facts tending to show non-equivalence. Examiner must ensure applicant's interpretation is consistent with the specification and weigh the indicia presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even if non-equivalence proven, perform obviousness (§103) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of non-equivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent the prior art element from rendering the claim limitation obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must still make a §103 analysis to determine whether claimed means or step-plus-function is obvious in view of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply §102/§103 rejections when equivalents scope uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the exact scope of an 'equivalent' may be uncertain, it is appropriate to apply a §102/§103 rejection where the balance of the claim limitations are anticipated by or render obvious the claimed invention based on the prior art relied on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although best practice is to rely on the best prior art references, alternative grounds of rejection may be appropriate when prior art shows differing elements that nonetheless perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'equivalent' in §112, 6th paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'equivalent' is generally interpreted as embracing more than the specific elements described in the specification for performing the specified function, but less than any element that performs the function specified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of equivalents depends on how the element is described in the supporting specification; the claim may or may not be limited to particular structure, material or acts depending on the specification's treatment. If the disclosure is so broad as to encompass any and all structures for the function, the limitation may effectively cover any element performing that function; conversely, a disclosure limited to a specific structure may constrict claim scope to the disclosed embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia to consider when determining equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that support a conclusion that one element is or is not an 'equivalent' include specific indicia rather than a single litmus test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicative factors include: (1) whether the prior art element performs the function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same results as the corresponding element in the specification; (2) whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the interchangeability of the prior art element for the disclosed element; (3) whether the prior art element is a structural equivalent performing the function in substantially the same manner; and (4) whether the disclosed structure/material/acts represent an insubstantial change adding nothing of significance to the prior art element. These examples are sufficient but not exhaustive; other indicia may be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh indicia; do not accept bare statements of non-equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether arguments or Rule 132 evidence are persuasive, the examiner should consider and weigh as many indicia as are presented and determine whether, on balance, the applicant has met the burden of proof to show non-equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under no circumstance should an examiner accept as persuasive a bare statement or opinion that the prior art element is not an equivalent embraced by the claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent improper narrowing by applicant without specification support
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant argues that 'means' or 'step' plus function language is limited to certain specific structural or additional functional characteristics where the specification does not describe the invention as being only those characteristics, the claim should not be allowed until amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must amend the claim to recite those specific structural or additional functional characteristics if they want the claim limited accordingly; otherwise claim allowance would provide inadequate public notice of true scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment options to overcome rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may amend the claim by further limiting the function so there is no longer identity of function with prior art, or may replace the claimed means-plus-function limitation with specific structure, material or acts not described in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments are an available avenue during prosecution to meet statutory criteria for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related §112, first and second paragraph rejections when no corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a means or step-plus-function limitation is not supported by corresponding structure, material or acts in the specification disclosure, consider rejections under: (1) §112, first paragraph (not enabled), (2) §112, second paragraph (indefinite), and (3) §102 or §103 where the prior art anticipates or renders obvious the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory: without corresponding structure in the specification to limit the limitation, an equivalent could be any element that performs the specified function. Note that block diagrams that describe function but not structure are not fatal under enablement if structure is conventional and determinable without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish §112,6th 'equivalents' from doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'equivalent' for §112, 6th paragraph should not be confused with the doctrine of equivalents (DOE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §112,6th limits the scope of means-or-step-plus-function language to structures, materials and acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof for claim construction during examination. DOE is an equitable doctrine applied in infringement litigation to expand exclusive rights beyond literal claim scope; DOE decisions should not unduly influence ex parte examination under §112,6th.
